📌 CONCLUSION: I talk all the time about freedom. I truly believe that the pursuit of freedom is why most of us go down this road in the first place. And the path that starts with investor money and ends with acqui-hire is pretty close to the polar opposite of the freedom we all seek.

What’s crazy to me is that most of the people in our ecosystem wouldn’t be happy with an RB2B outcome. Simple product, simple business, stalls at $10m, but requires very little ongoing human effort. Can’t sell it, but generates millions of cash to fund our next experiment, and freedom to do whatever you want is the max it could be.

But somehow the news cycle, peer groups, and investors tap into our ambition, ego, and greed, and make most people think RB2B is silly, cute, or boring.

I wonder if at any point after enough acqui-hires (or worse) people in our ecosystem will step back and ask “WHY” …

Why do we need to grow forever?
Why do we need to tie our future to capital market transactions?
Why do we need to burn tons of money, hoping the next round materializes?

When none of that is in service of true freedom.

Maybe someday the boring path of slowly growing cash flow will be in style…

But I doubt it.
Bethany Stachenfeld yea that is also true. I just want to advertise the bootstrap side which gets zero airtime. People should at least know what’s possible when they have the option.
Sachin Gupta if you think I am beating them up, you have not followed me for long

📌 THE 4 SKILLS THAT MATTER NOW (cont'd)

I believe that hundreds of millions of tiny verticalized companies that are some hybrid between prompting LLMs and software will pop up to solve very specific workflows. 

Tiny, indie, lifestyle businesses. 

The ones you actually hear about will probably look a lot like RB2B… 

They’ll have the “Kardashian effect” of somebody who understands how to harness the power of organic social media and direct it towards their “app”. 

I think if you: 

- Get incredibly good at prompting, and
- Get incredibly good at organic social media, and
- Get incredibly good at evaluating the strength of an idea, and
- Get incredibly good at communicating a clear vision to an engineer

You are positioned very well for the coming boom of verticalized LLM prompting tiny workflow apps.

📌 WHERE THE OPPORTUNITIES ARE

1. Look at heavy software suites where a point solution is 80% of the value they are selling

2. Look at verticalized solutions in one vertical that could be copied elsewhere or niched down on (legal >>> real estate law )

3. Look for things everybody uses where an insane amount of manual work is still required (ie quickbooks)

4. Look for spaces that have easy-to-access customer lists (builtwith, etc)

5. Bonus points if you can hit a space where YOU are actually your buyer persona … b/c the organic social media flywheel will help you take off

👇

📌 HOW YOU SHOULD GO TO MARKET 

1. Founder-Led Organic Social for TOFU
2. Freemium PLG, low-priced entry point
3. Play the long game w/ data moats and network effects if you can

The idea should be to acquire as many users as possible in a high-velocity, low-friction model. 

If you succeed, it’s very difficult to undercut something like this.

📌 WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE 

The dream of every founder should be a growing, highly-profitable, lean machine, where you pay yourself millions of dollars and don’t have to answer to ANYBODY. Why? 

Because $10m ARR is the FU money of SaaS … 

And FREEDOM is the most valuable thing in our short lives.

In the coming years you’ll be able to bootstrap your way there quicker than ever with ever-fewer resources required. 

I sit here writing these words so that YOU will know that all this is possible … 

Everything that we’re experiencing right now with RB2B and Retention.com

And it’s a WAY better outcome for you than what everyone you know is doing. 

It’s the bootstrapper vs. YC model. 

And in 2026 and beyond, the bootstrapper wins.
Fajar Fatima I think the danger now is over-building
Alina Vandenberghe 🌶️ you will be paving the way!

📌 Stay Manual As Long As Possible

I’d only build what's needed to deliver the core value proposition. If it takes more than 4-6 weeks, I'm building too much.

Everything I want to build but could do manually, I'd do manually at first.
With RB2B, we manually sent spreadsheets over email for 5 months before we even put up a website. We could have built automation tools, but we didn't.

Staying manual kept us incredibly close to customers. We learned things we'd never discover with automation, and we iterated 10x faster than competitors trying to automate everything.

Manual processes are your unfair advantage.

📌  3 Signals I’d Look For

1. At least one referral per week from paying customers.
2. Customers would be genuinely upset if I took the product away.
3. Organic growth without doing any marketing.

If I don't have all 3, I don't have PMF yet. And until I have these signals, I wouldn't do anything else besides try to get PMF.

Nothing else will work without it.

Once you start seeing organic traffic, you need to know who's visiting your site. That's when you'd want to see exactly who's checking you out.

Start identifying your website visitors for free here: rb2b.com

📌  Build In Public From Day One

I’d post on LinkedIn from day one. Share the building journey in real time - wins, failures, pivots.

This creates awareness so that when I start outreach, people already know who I am.

With RB2B, I spent months building in public on LinkedIn before we even launched. By launch, we had a 1,600-person waitlist and 300 meetings booked.

That early content let us hit $1M ARR in just 6 weeks post-launch.

📌 The Magic Triangle

Once I have PMF, I'd activate 3 channels: Content, outreach, and retargeting.

Each channel feeds the other two.

Content drives awareness and generates web traffic.

Outreach converts those warm website visitors.

Retargeting brings back people who weren't ready yet.

Content alone is too slow.

Outbound alone has terrible conversion rates - cold email is basically dead.

Retargeting alone doesn't generate a new pipeline.

But together, they create a compounding engine.

📌 How I’d Do Outreach

2 types of outreach:

1. Cold outreach only to people in my ICP. I'd use Apollo for lists of founders and marketers at SaaS companies from 5 to 200 employees. 3 people per company.

2. Warm outreach to people visiting my website. That's why I built RB2B.

After you install it, RB2B identifies your anonymous website visitors at the person level. First name, job title, LinkedIn profile, business email.

Instead of cold outreach, you're following up with people who already showed interest.

For email, I'd use Instantly or Smartlead and rotate hundreds of domains. 2 inboxes per domain, sending 2-10 emails per day from each. This low volume lets emails sneak past spam filters.

For LinkedIn, I'd connect with 10-20 prospects daily. Connection requests with no messages - acceptance rates are high, especially for website visitors.

After they accept, I'd wait for them to engage with my content. Once they like or comment: “Hey [first name]. Thanks for the like. How are things going at [company]?”

Response rate is usually north of 60%.

I'd never sell on LinkedIn. Just build rapport to get them on a call.

📌 Retargeting Ties It Together

I’d install pixels from LinkedIn, Meta, Google, and Twitter. Create custom audiences from website visitors and lookalike audiences from paying customers.

For ad creative, I'd use the who, what, why, how framework:   Who are you?  What do you have?  Why do they need it?  How can they get it?

Keep it authentic. Selfie videos I record on my phone actually perform best.

This is what makes the magic triangle work.
